title: One approved anchor picture per character, reused everywhere
rule: Choose one approved picture of each character before any video is made and feed that same picture to every picture and clip that shows the character.
why: The first clear appearance sets the ceiling for consistency, and an ablation without picture anchors collapsed the consistency score from 7.99 to 0.55; each fresh generation is otherwise a new sample.
how: Make 3 candidates, let a human pick one, lock it, attach it to every later request. Do not swap it mid-film unless the character really changes look.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFace (candidates A/B/C, anchor) and makeFrame (anchors from each character's chosen face)

title: Plain, neutral reference portrait of exactly one character
rule: Draw the reference with one character, a plain neutral background, looking slightly off camera, with nothing in the hands and no extra people.
why: Models copy what they see in a reference (background, pose, props); clean single-subject references give steadier identity and held objects differ between turnaround angles.
how: Prompt shape: 'Portrait of one character, head and shoulders, plain neutral background, facing slightly off camera, no text', then the description.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFace prompt ('plain neutral background', 'not a person holding or dressed as it')

title: Add a second and third view to the reference set
rule: Give the generator at least two views of each main character (front or three-quarter plus a full-body or profile), not one head-and-shoulders portrait.
why: Veo, Kling and Runway all take several references; head-and-shoulders alone does not show outfit, proportions or the side of the head, and the model invents what it cannot see. Similar-looking references can also cause drift.
how: After the face is approved, edit it into a full-body view and a profile view with 'same character, same outfit, proportions and art style identical', and attach the set (Veo up to 3, Kling element up to 4 images).

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeView (full-body and side view drawn from the chosen face and checked against it); Roll camera step "views"; get_clip lists the views after the faces; the People page shows them

title: Do not re-describe the character in words when a picture already carries it
rule: When a start picture or reference image exists, write the clip prompt about motion, camera and place only, and refer to the character by name as 'exactly as in the picture'.
why: Words and picture are two sources of truth; the model blends them and the face shifts. Wan and Sora guidance say the image decides how things look, the prompt only what moves.
how: 'Mimi looks exactly as in the start picture, same clothes, colours and shapes in every frame. She walks to the door and looks back.'

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js composeClip (film.pictures: names only, no description)

title: Without a picture, repeat a fixed identity line word for word
rule: In text-only generation, put the same identity sentence (age, face and hair, signature clothing) first in every prompt and change only action, camera and setting.
why: Small wording changes between prompts make the model reinterpret the character; vague definitions let it improvise.
how: '[28-year-old woman, short black bob, round glasses, mustard raincoat], [action], [camera], [place and light]'. Keep attribute order and vocabulary identical.

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js composeClip (no-picture branch lists 'Name: desc' for each character)
monofilm.idea: Keep the description text frozen after approval so every prompt reuses it exactly.

title: Name the outfit if the picture may not show it
rule: If a garment or accessory is not clearly visible in the reference, name it in the prompt; if it is visible, rely on the picture.
why: Unspecified clothing is improvised; but extra adjectives that clash with the picture cause flipping, so only state what the picture cannot show.
how: Fix a vague picture by editing the picture, not by piling on words; use 'wearing the same blue jacket' only as a short reminder.

monofilm.where: src/picturecheck.js compares clothes and colours against the reference; composeClip omits descriptions when pictures exist
monofilm.idea: Let the review ask for a corrected start picture rather than extra prompt words.

title: Check every new picture against the reference, garment by garment
rule: Compare each character in a new picture with its reference picture on clothes, colours, body or ear shape and markings, and reject on any difference.
why: Identity drift shows first in outfit and colour; a written check word by word ('blue overalls are not a pink sweater') is more reliable than a glance.
how: Send the picture and the reference to a vision model; ask it to list what it sees per character before deciding; second look before failing.

monofilm.where: src/picturecheck.js checkPicture (reference pictures after the first, kind 'appearance', second opinion)

title: Judge clips against the start and end pictures, not against the words
rule: When reviewing a clip, compare sampled frames with the approved start and end pictures as ground truth, and compare at every cut with the original reference, not only the previous clip.
why: Chained comparisons let small errors pass one by one; the anchor is the standard.
how: Pass 4 to 8 frames plus the pictures to the reviewer; report any look change as 'identity'.

monofilm.where: src/takereview.js SYSTEM and reviewFrames (pictures as ground truth, kind 'identity')

title: Score face identity with embeddings, and calibrate on your own footage
rule: Where the character has a real or realistic face, add a numeric check: cosine similarity of face embeddings (ArcFace) between sampled frames and the approved reference, with a threshold set from your own good and bad takes.
why: Embedding distances separate real video (ArcFace 0.08) from generated video (0.17 to 0.48 across models); there is no universal cutoff and numbers are not tied to human judgement.
how: Detect the face in 5 to 8 frames, skip frames with no face, take the minimum and the mean similarity; flag takes below the calibrated line and send them to the VLM check.

monofilm.where: src/takereview.js uses a vision model only
monofilm.idea: Add an optional face-embedding score next to the vision check for person characters; keep the vision check for cartoons and animals.

title: Make the review compare against known failure kinds
rule: Ask the reviewer specific questions: face shape and hairline, outfit and accessories, light, style finish, proportions, and whether the face holds through head turns.
why: A checklist catches the drift types practitioners report (face, outfit, accessories, lighting, style) instead of a vague 'looks fine'.
how: Use the checklist for both picture and clip reviews; test head turns and expressions early.

monofilm.where: src/picturecheck.js (clothes, colours, shapes) and src/takereview.js (identity); no head-turn or proportion item
monofilm.idea: Add proportions and 'face through head turns' to the clip review list.

title: Keep clips short and motion moderate
rule: Use short clips (about 4 to 10 seconds), limit large motion, and use start and end frames for controlled movement.
why: Identity breaks under big pose or expression changes and small faces; model reports show drift grows with motion and length.
how: Split long beats into several clips from approved pictures; calm the camera before shrinking the face.

monofilm.where: public/js/wizard-model.js clipPlan, timingLine
monofilm.idea: Reduce the maximum clip length when a character has a small face in frame.

title: Do not edit an edit; return to the anchor
rule: If a character drifts after several editing turns, restart from the approved anchor with the full description instead of editing the latest image again.
why: Iterative editing degrades character consistency across turns; Google advises a fresh conversation with a detailed description.
how: Keep the edit chain to one or two steps; one change per prompt ('She is now holding an umbrella'); for end pictures, also pass the anchor face.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFrame (end picture is made FROM the previous picture, plus the anchor faces)
monofilm.idea: Always pass the anchor face, never only the previous frame, and cap the chain length.

title: Use plain references and varied angles to avoid copy-paste
rule: Provide clean references with the background cleared, and use more than one angle so the model learns identity and not the reference's pose, light and background.
why: Research names copy-paste: models absorb pose, lighting and layout of a single reference and ignore the prompt; multi-angle or clip references reduce it.
how: If outputs copy the reference pose or background, replace one reference with a different angle and strip the background.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFace (plain background); only one angle
monofilm.idea: Add a profile or three-quarter reference to break pose locking.

title: Make characters in the same scene visibly different
rule: When two or more characters share a frame, design them with different height, palette, body shape and costume silhouette, and give each its own reference.
why: Models average the features of characters in one frame into one hybrid; ambiguity invites it, and tools accept one reference per character (Kling up to four images).
how: Separate sheet per character; pass all references plus the place picture in one call; for contact scenes, add a sketch of who touches whom.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFrame passes anchors per character; no check that characters differ
monofilm.idea: Warn at casting when two characters share silhouette or colours; add a 'distinct from' rule to the cast prompt.

title: For multi-character shots, expect many takes and cut the best seconds
rule: Budget about three generations per usable shot for contact scenes, and cut between takes where each character looks right.
why: One vendor reports roughly 25% of takes used; blending is hard to prompt away.
how: Keep the contact moment short; cover it with a cut or a reaction shot.

monofilm.where: src/takereview.js retry flow (retry count ignores takes made before the scene changed)

title: Non-human characters: say the being, and keep the style in the reference
rule: For animals, creatures and toys, state the kind of being and the medium, and draw the character itself, not a person holding or dressed as it.
why: Reference tools accept non-human subjects (creatures, animals, toys), but a vague prompt gets a human or a photo; looser strength settings are meant for stylised characters.
how: 'Illustration of one penguin character, not a person, not a toy.' Check 'being' and 'medium' after drawing.

monofilm.where: src/wizard.js makeFace (thing = character), src/picturecheck.js kinds 'being' and 'medium'

title: Match reference strength to the job
rule: Use a high reference weight when face or outfit must hold, and a lower one when the style should change; do not push the weight to the maximum by default.
why: Midjourney reports high values keep face and clothes but moderate values avoid quality loss; Luma's Adhere/Reimagine slider trades shape fidelity against freedom.
how: Start at the default; raise to about 400 (Midjourney) for faces; lower for restyling; test on one clip.

monofilm.where: none: the studio does not set a reference weight
monofilm.idea: Expose a reference-strength choice per generator profile when a model supports it.

title: Screen-test the reference before the full production
rule: Run the approved reference through 3 to 5 different scenes, light conditions and head angles before generating the film.
why: Cheap tests show whether the reference holds across views; failing references can be replaced early, or a different model chosen.
how: One short clip per main character with a head turn and a change of light; keep a rejection list.

monofilm.where: none
monofilm.idea: Add a 'screen test' step after the face is approved.

title: Train a character LoRA only with a varied, consistent dataset
rule: If you train a LoRA for a character, use about 15 to 30 (image models) or at least 10 (Wan) on-subject images with varied background, light and angle, one trigger token, and pick an earlier checkpoint when it overfits.
why: The model learns whatever stays constant; repeated pose or outfit makes it impossible to change clothing; Higgsfield says a small clean varied set beats a big inconsistent one.
how: Caption what varies, leave the identity out of captions; compare checkpoints on the same seed; test LoRA scale 0.6 to 1.0.

monofilm.where: none (the studio uses reference pictures, not LoRAs)
monofilm.idea: Out of scope for now; keep as an option for a recurring series character.

title: Use training-free adapters when only one photo exists
rule: When only one face photo exists, prefer identity adapters (IP-Adapter, InstantID, PuLID, or video versions like ID-Animator and Stand-In) to per-subject fine-tuning.
why: They need no per-subject training and give identity in a single pass; fine-tuning (DreamBooth, LoRA) costs time and storage.
how: Face-only adapters do not hold outfit or body; add the outfit through the picture.

monofilm.where: none (the studio calls hosted generators)
monofilm.idea: Note in generator profiles which models have a face-ID mode.

title: New look means a new reference sheet
rule: When a character changes outfit, gains an injury or a prop, make a new reference for that look and use it from that scene on.
why: The old sheet becomes inaccurate and the model keeps producing the old look.
how: Treat each look as a separate cast entry linked to the character.

monofilm.where: none: one anchor face per character
monofilm.idea: Support per-scene looks as variants of a cast member.

title: Order reference images and match their shape to the output
rule: Give references in the aspect ratio of the output, and note that some models take the shape of the last image.
why: Gemini's output adopts the last uploaded image's ratio when they differ.
how: Make references in the film's aspect or include a blank image of the right size last.

title: Save the best take early and cap re-rolls
rule: Save an approved result as soon as it is good and stop after about 3 to 4 re-rolls of the same shot.
why: Re-rolls accumulate variations and each is a fresh sample.
how: If it still fails, change the reference or the model, not the same prompt.

title: Do not trust words or references to carry size; fix scale in the picture
rule: Treat size as something the image model will not obey from words or from reference pictures; set it by construction (a layout, a composite or an edit that starts from a picture that already has the right sizes).
why: A user got 1.1x instead of the asked 1.4x height ratio across 15 phrasings and a reference with the right ratio, while plain text-to-image gave 1.4x; GenScale finds no tested generator or editor reliable on relative scale (best 56.5% plausible on common objects).
how: Draw the scene (or a lineup of all its characters at the right sizes) first, then apply identity in an edit turn; describe height by body alignment (where one head reaches on the other) rather than a ratio number; say references are for face and clothing only; check by measurement.

monofilm.where: makeLineup in src/wizard.js: a scale sheet of the scene's characters is drawn once per scene and goes into every picture of the scene as a reference (role scale in src/tools.js)

title: Normalise references to one common scale before they enter a scene
rule: Give every reference of a scene the same framing and zoom level, and one picture that shows the characters side by side at the right relative size.
why: Reference images that differ in zoom make subjects come out unnaturally large or small in multi-subject generation (MoFu). Vendor advice is a reference at a neutral focal length with the subject inside the central 60% of the frame.
how: Crop or redraw per-character references so the character fills the same fraction of the frame; keep the lineup picture as the size source.

monofilm.where: references are per character (face, outfit); no common-scale rule
monofilm.idea: Normalise reference crops and add the lineup picture.
